evidence.label: Stabilizer orbits and thick tensor ideals of dualizable K(n)-local spectra

headline: Claims Chai's invariant-ideal conjecture at every prime and height, and with it the Hovey–Strickland classification.
scope: Lubin–Tate rings over finite residue fields at every prime and positive height n, and dualizable K(n)-local spectra.
plain: Chromatic homotopy theory splits stable homotopy theory into layers indexed by a height n. Hovey and Strickland conjectured that one layer's dualizable objects have exactly n+2 thick tensor ideals, a list of closed families. Barthel, Heard and Naumann showed this would follow from Chai's conjecture about symmetric ideals in a ring of power series. This paper claims Chai's conjecture at every prime and height. So it also claims the Hovey–Strickland count.
doesNot: This does not classify ideals in the larger category of all K(n)-local spectra, only the dualizable ones.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Mark Hovey and Neil Strickland, Morava K-theories and localisation
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims two linked conjectures at every height, where the spectral one was known only at height two.

explanation:
Start with a ring of power series. At height n = 3 it is E₀ = W(F_{p³})[[u₁, u₂]]. Here W(F_{p³}) is a ring of p-adic integers built from a finite field with p³ elements. This ring has many prime ideals, the basic building blocks of its ideals. But a large symmetry group acts on it, called the Morava stabilizer group. Only some ideals stay fixed under that action. There are obvious ones, the height ideals: 0, (p), (p, u₁) and (p, u₁, u₂). That is n + 1 = 4 fixed primes. Adding the whole ring gives 5 fixed radical ideals, which is n + 2.

Chai proposed that the fixed loci should be exactly these height loci[10]. The paper claims that the fixed proper prime ideals are exactly 0 and the height ideals[3]. This holds for every open subgroup of the stabilizer, which extends the earlier formulation[9]. So the paper claims Chai's conjecture in its standard form[1]. The hard part is the layers in characteristic p. There, small symmetry directions alone do not control the fixed equations[7].

Why does this matter for topology? Hopkins and Smith classified the thick subcategories of finite spectra by chromatic type[6]. A thick subcategory is a family closed under the basic building moves. Hovey and Strickland proposed the same kind of list for dualizable K(n)-local spectra[5]. Dualizable objects have a well-behaved dual. This class is larger than the compact objects[8]. Barthel, Heard and Naumann proved this list at height two. They also showed that Chai's conjecture would give it at every height[4].

With that implication, the paper claims the Hovey–Strickland conjecture. The dualizable K(n)-local category has exactly n + 2 thick tensor ideals. Its Balmer spectrum, the space of prime ideals, is a chain of n + 1 points[2]. At height 3 that is 5 ideals and 4 points. This matches the 4 fixed primes in the example above.

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The proof uses deep tools from p-adic geometry. The topological part relies on the earlier Barthel–Heard–Naumann implication. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. The topological conclusion depends on earlier published work. There is no Lean check and no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: The index n of a layer in chromatic homotopy theory.
An ideal that plays the role of a prime number in a ring.
An ideal that contains every element some power of which lies in it.
A large symmetry group that acts on the Lubin–Tate ring.
A family of objects closed under the basic building moves and under tensoring with anything.
An object with a well-behaved dual, so that maps out of it match maps into its dual.
The space of prime thick tensor ideals of a tensor category.
